```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# The calibration runs below take about 20 minutes on 8 cores, so the code
# chunks are not run when the vignette is built. Their results were saved by
# dev/precompute-calibration.R and are read from calibration-results.rds.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%")
library(crywolf)
results <- readRDS("calibration-results.rds")
cal_fit_res <- readRDS("calibration-fit-results.rds")
```

```{r stale, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat(crywolf:::.stale_note(results, "calibration-results.rds"),
    crywolf:::.stale_note(cal_fit_res, "calibration-fit-results.rds"),
    crywolf:::.stale_note(readRDS("sbc-results.rds"), "sbc-results.rds"), sep = "")
```

A 95% credible interval should contain the true value in about 95% of
datasets. When the model is misspecified, it may not, and nothing in a
single fit will warn you. Simulation-based calibration answers the question
for a given design: simulate many datasets from known parameters, fit the
model to each, and count how often the intervals cover the truth. This is
a coverage-based form of simulation-based calibration checking, one of the
steps of the Bayesian workflow (Gelman et al., 2026, Ch. 31).

## The workflow

1. Describe the design you can afford: number of sites, automated occasions,
   fraction of sites verified, and plausible detection and false-positive
   rates.
2. Describe the false-positive structure you suspect: homogeneous, random
   among sites, or tracking an environmental gradient.
3. Run `fp_calibrate()` with the candidate models.
4. Read the coverage and bias of the quantity you care about, usually the
   occupancy slope.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(crywolf)
fp_compile()   # compile once before starting parallel workers

future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 8)

design <- expand.grid(
  nsite = 300, nocc = 20, p10 = 0.05, frac_verified = 0.3,
  conf_effect = c(0, 0.5, 1.5), conf_cor = 0.7
)

cal <- fp_calibrate(
  design,
  models = list(constant = ~ 1, fp_on_x = ~ x),
  occ = ~ x, reps = 50, parallel = TRUE
)
summary(cal)
```

The code above is not run when this vignette is built; the output below
comes from the same call, saved in advance. `summary()` prints, for the
occupancy slope, the coverage of the 95% intervals, its Monte Carlo standard
error, the bias, and a verdict:

```{r results-confusion, echo = FALSE}
summary(results$confusion)
```

```{r plot-confusion, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Coverage of the 95% interval of the occupancy slope against the strength of the confusion, for the constant-rate model and for a false-positive rate that depends on the occupancy covariate. Bars span two Monte Carlo standard errors; the dashed line is the nominal coverage."}
plot(results$confusion, by = "conf_effect")
```

Each replicate costs one Stan fit per model, so this design needs
3 cells × 50 replicates × 2 models = 300 fits. With 50 replicates, the Monte
Carlo standard error of a coverage of 0.95 is about 0.03, enough to tell a
calibrated model from a broken one; raise `reps` only to pin a borderline
value. Every model is fitted to the same datasets, so comparisons between
models are paired. Inside each worker the chains of a fit run one after
another, so `fit_args = list(chains = 2, parallel_chains = 1)` takes half
the time of four chains; two chains of 1000 draws gave an effective sample
size of about 2000 per parameter in the default design, enough to place the
bounds of a 95% interval. The fixed cost of starting CmdStan and reading
its output was 0.4 to 1.1 seconds per fit.

The column `prop_divergent` is the share of fits with at least one divergent
transition. In this run only 2 of the 800 fits had one, and the largest
R-hat was 1.01. Check `max_rhat` and `divergences` in the returned tibble
before trusting a cell whose fits had many. The simulated designs here have
no recorder effect, so the calibration fits leave the recorder random
intercept out; fitting a random effect whose true variance is zero is a
common source of divergent transitions.

## How much to verify

Verification anchors the false-positive rate. It is natural to think that
verifying more sites will rescue a model that is not calibrated, and
`fp_verification_curve()` tests that directly:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fp_verification_curve(
  nsite = 300, nocc = 20, p10 = 0.05, conf_effect = 1.5, conf_cor = 0.7,
  frac_verified = c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9),
  models = list(constant = ~ 1, fp_on_x = ~ x),
  reps = 50, parallel = TRUE
)
```

```{r results-verification, echo = FALSE}
summary(results$verification)
```

```{r plot-verification, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Coverage of the 95% interval of the occupancy slope against the fraction of sites verified, under structured confusion (effect 1.5, correlation 0.7)."}
plot(results$verification)
```

## What to expect

In the simulation study that motivated this package (Provete et al., in
preparation), at a base false-positive rate of 0.05:

* When false positives were homogeneous, the constant-rate model kept nominal
  coverage of the occupancy slope. When they varied at random among sites,
  the estimate of the false-positive rate became unreliable, but coverage of
  the slope fell only to 0.81 (across all cells of that regime).
* When the false-positive rate tracked a gradient correlated with the
  occupancy covariate (effect 1.5 on the logit scale, correlation 0.7),
  coverage of the slope fell to 0.08–0.20, and verifying up to 90% of the
  sites did not restore it.
* Letting the false-positive rate depend on the occupancy covariate
  (`fp = ~ x`) recovered part of the coverage (0.48–0.66) and improved with
  verification; with the true gradient (`fp = ~ w`), coverage returned to
  0.90–0.97.
* Weak confusion (effects of 0.5 or less) left the constant-rate model
  calibrated at every correlation, including when false positives depended on
  the occupancy covariate itself.

So, if `fp_verification_curve()` shows the constant-rate model stuck below
nominal coverage, verifying more is not the remedy. Model the false-positive
rate instead, and verify enough to tell its effect apart from the occupancy
effect.

## Calibrating a fitted model

The checks above describe a planned design with simulated covariates.
Once a model has been fitted to real data, `fp_calibrate_fit()` asks the
same question for data like the real ones: it simulates datasets from the
fit with `simulate()`, keeping the sites, covariates, occasions, recorders,
and verification of the real data, refits each candidate model to every
dataset, and scores the coverage and bias of their intervals. The cost is
that of refitting the real data `reps` times per model.

A typical use pits the model you fitted against a simpler one. If a model
in which the false-positive rate depends on a measured gradient found a
clear effect, data simulated from it show whether a constant rate would
have biased the occupancy effects at your sample size and verification
effort. Here the "real" data are one simulated dataset with structured
confusion (300 sites, 20 occasions, 30% of sites verified), and the model
of interest lets the false-positive rate depend on the gradient `w`
(`dev/precompute-calibration-fit.R`):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
sim <- simulate_fp(nsite = 300, nocc = 20, p10 = 0.05, frac_verified = 0.3,
                   conf_effect = 1.5, conf_cor = 0.7, seed = 1)
m_w <- fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ w, random_recorder = FALSE,
               threads_per_chain = 1, seed = 1)
cal_fit <- fp_calibrate_fit(m_w, models = list(constant = ~ 1, fp_w = ~ w),
                            reps = 50, parallel = TRUE)
summary(cal_fit)
plot(cal_fit, parameter = "occ_x")
```

```{r calibration-fit-summary, echo = FALSE}
cal_fit <- cal_fit_res$calibration
summary(cal_fit)
```

```{r calibration-fit-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Coverage of the 95% interval of the occupancy slope in 50 datasets simulated from the fitted model with fp = ~ w, refitted with a constant false-positive rate and with fp = ~ w. Bars span two Monte Carlo standard errors; the dashed line is the nominal coverage."}
plot(cal_fit, parameter = "occ_x")
```

```{r calibration-fit-numbers, include = FALSE}
cf <- summary(cal_fit)
cf <- as.data.frame(cf)
row <- function(model, col) cf[cf$model == model & cf$parameter == "occ_x", col]
```

In data like these, a constant false-positive rate would have missed the
occupancy slope: its 95% interval covered the true value in
`r sprintf("%.2f", row("constant", "coverage"))` of the datasets, with a
bias of `r sprintf("%+.2f", row("constant", "bias"))`, whereas the model
with `fp = ~ w` covered it in `r sprintf("%.2f", row("fp_w", "coverage"))`
(bias `r sprintf("%+.2f", row("fp_w", "bias"))`), somewhat below the
nominal 0.95 (the Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage near 0.9 with 50
replicates is about 0.04). The check refitted the data 100 times, two
models by 50 replicates.

By default every dataset is simulated from the posterior means;
`truth = "posterior"` draws a different set of parameter values from the
posterior for each dataset, so that the check also reflects how uncertain
the fit was. Either way, the check covers only the structure of the
generating model: a dependence of the false-positive rate on a variable
that was not measured is not part of it.

## Is the computation right?

All the checks above take for granted that the sampler finds the posterior
of the model. Simulation-based calibration tests that assumption on its
own (Talts et al., 2018; Modrák et al., 2025; Gelman et al., 2026, Ch. 31):
`fp_sbc()` draws parameter values from the priors, simulates data with the
design at hand, fits the model, and records the rank of each true value
among the posterior draws. It also ranks the log-likelihood of the
simulated data at the true values among its values at the draws
(`log_lik`), a test quantity that depends on the data and catches problems
the parameter ranks can miss (Modrák et al., 2025). When the computation
is right, the ranks are uniform.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
sbc <- fp_sbc(sim$data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1, random_recorder = FALSE,
              reps = 200, parallel = TRUE)
summary(sbc)
```

```{r sbc, echo = FALSE}
sbc <- readRDS("sbc-results.rds")
summary(sbc)
```

```{r plot-sbc, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Ranks of the true values among 99 posterior draws in 200 replicates of simulation-based calibration (80 sites, 6 occasions, constant false-positive rate). The grey band is the 99% range of each bin's count under uniform ranks."}
plot(sbc)
```

The ranks look uniform for every quantity. The gap has the lowest p-value,
`r sprintf("%.3f", min(summary(sbc)$p_uniform))`, which is not small once
`r nrow(summary(sbc))` quantities are tested at once (the Bonferroni
threshold for a 5% level is
`r sprintf("%.3f", 0.05 / nrow(summary(sbc)))`); a larger run would tell
whether its slight excess of high ranks is real. The chi-squared test of
binned ranks is coarse, so the histograms are worth a look as well. This
differs from the coverage checks of `fp_calibrate()`: there, data come from
fixed parameter values that may break the model's assumptions; here, they
come from the model itself, so only the computation is under test.

## Plotting

`plot()` draws the coverage of the occupancy slope against the design column
that varies (here, the fraction of sites verified), one colour per model,
with intervals of two Monte Carlo standard errors and a dashed line at the
nominal level. `type = "bias"` plots the bias instead, and `parameter`
selects another scored quantity. The result is a 'ggplot2' object that can be
modified as usual.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plot(cal)
plot(cal, type = "bias")
plot(cal, parameter = "p10_bar")
```

For the verification curve above, the bias of the occupancy slope shows why
coverage stays low: the constant-rate model overestimates the slope at every
level of verification, and modelling the rate on `x` reduces, but does not
remove, the bias.

```{r plot-bias, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Bias of the posterior mean of the occupancy slope against the fraction of sites verified, under structured confusion (effect 1.5, correlation 0.7). The dashed line marks no bias."}
plot(results$verification, type = "bias")
```

```{r plot-p10, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Coverage of the 95% interval of the mean false-positive rate over sites (`p10_bar`), in the same simulations."}
plot(results$verification, parameter = "p10_bar")
```

Neither model recovers the mean false-positive rate over sites under this
confusion. Both estimate it at about 0.077 when the truth is about 0.10,
with intervals only about 0.02 wide, so coverage stays at 0.22 or below at
every level of verification. Modelling the rate on `x` reduces the bias of
the occupancy slope, but a rate that depends on the unmeasured gradient `w`
is not fully captured by `x`.
